summary:
Saint Helena is a British Overseas Territory. United Kingdom legislation reaches it only where extended by order, so the territory's own ordinances and institutions, not United Kingdom law, determine what a visitor encounters. No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care or violence provision is documented in territory law.

Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha. No penalty provision specific to transgender people is documented.

The St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha Constitution Order 2009 bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and has been in force since 2009. It defines "discriminatory" as affording different treatment to different persons on any ground such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status. The enumerated grounds do not include gender reassignment, and no extension of the ban to gender reassignment is documented.

The Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015 defines "gender reassignment" as an intended, current or past process, or part of such a process, for reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex, or the state of mind whereby a person psychologically identifies with a gender inconsistent with, or not culturally associated with, their assigned sex at birth. The same ordinance defines sexual orientation as a person's orientation towards persons of the same sex, the opposite sex, or either sex.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes understanding of the importance of equality, and works towards the elimination of unlawful discrimination. It may conduct inquiries and investigations into persons suspected of having committed an unlawful act, including unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender reassignment.

Same-sex marriage is legal on Ascension Island under the Marriage (Ascension) Ordinance 2016, approved by the Ascension Island Council on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0, signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016, and commenced on 1 January 2017. On Tristan da Cunha it has been legal since 4 August 2017 under the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance 2017, which defines marriage as the union of two persons regardless of sex and extends eligibility, formalities, rights and recognition to same-sex couples on equal terms with opposite-sex couples. On Saint Helena it has been legal since 20 December 2017 under the Marriage Ordinance 2017; the first same-sex marriage there took place on 31 December 2018. No marriage provision specific to transgender people is documented.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017. Under the Saint Helena Welfare of Children Ordinance 2010, covering Saint Helena and Tristan da Cunha, and the Ascension Island Child Welfare Ordinance 2011, single and married people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation. No adoption provision specific to transgender people is documented.
tangentialFactors:
The territory is classified as an Overseas Country or Territory of the European Union, and the applicability of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights is recorded on that basis.

Marriage was legislated separately by each of the three constituent parts rather than by a single territory-wide instrument, so recognition is uniform in effect but rests on three ordinances.

Protection against discrimination sits at two levels: the 2009 Constitution Order's enumerated grounds, which cover sex and sexual orientation but not gender reassignment, and the 2015 ordinance, which supplies a definition of gender reassignment and gives the Commission jurisdiction over it. A visitor or resident relying on the constitutional ground alone would find gender reassignment outside its list.
localsOnly:
The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena is the body residents approach over suspected unlawful discrimination, including discrimination on the basis of gender reassignment, and it holds inquiry and investigation powers over persons suspected of committing an unlawful act.

Adoption is available in law to single and married people regardless of sexual orientation, but a 2006 United Kingdom Government report recorded no adoptions in Saint Helena or Ascension Island for many years. That report does not cover Tristan da Cunha.

Marriage recognition for residents rests on three separate ordinances, and the Tristan da Cunha instrument places same-sex couples on equal terms with opposite-sex couples for eligibility, formalities, rights and recognition.
outOfScopeNotes:
No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care or violence provision is documented for Saint Helena, Ascension Island or Tristan da Cunha. The absence of documented provisions is not evidence that no differential practice exists; it records that the sources consulted do not describe one.

Whether the Constitution Order 2009's sexual-orientation ground has been extended to gender reassignment is not documented, and no transgender-specific marriage, adoption or penalty provision is recorded.

One source, GayLawNet, was accessed on 23 June 2013, and its account of the territory's European Union Overseas Country or Territory status and EU Charter applicability is recorded on that basis. Another source is current to 25 April 2026.
